CANONICAL_NAME.value: Spacewar! 2B (25 March 1962) -- Steve Russell et al., MIT, for the DEC PDP-1

VERSION.value: spacewar 2b, 25 Mar 1962 (authentic source, as published by masswerk.at)

value.lineage: Written in 1961-62 by Steve Russell, Martin Graetz, Wayne Wiitanen and others on MIT's PDP-1, with the starfield (Expensive Planetarium) by Peter Samson and gravity by Dan Edwards. Two ships under player control orbit a central star; thrust, rotation, torpedoes and hyperspace are computed in real time on an 18-bit machine with 4096 words of core and a Type 30 point-plotting CRT. Widely held to be the first widely distributed digital video game. The body preserved here is the AUTHENTIC 25 Mar 1962 assembly listing, not the later reconstructed-from-binary variant, which masswerk publishes separately.

HUMAN_PROBLEM.value: real-time interactive simulation on a machine with no OS and no spare cycles

value.built_to: demonstrate what an interactive computer with a CRT could do, by making two human-controlled ships duel under real gravity in real time
value.pressure: 18-bit words, 4096 words of core, no floating point, no operating system, and a display that must be refreshed by the program itself while the game logic runs
value.success_means: the simulation stays responsive and the orbits remain believable within the machine's cycle budget

value.pressure: scarce core, scarce cycles, program-refreshed display, no floating point
value.failure_condition: the display flickers or the game slows as object count rises; integer overflow distorts the orbits

evidence.ref: Graetz, The Origin of Spacewar, Creative Computing 1981
evidence.says: Describes Spacewar's creation on the PDP-1 at MIT and its spread to other PDP-1 installations; the program is tied to that machine and its display.
Spacewar is demonstrated on a restored PDP-1 because the machine it requires is no longer in ordinary existence; roughly 53 PDP-1s were built.

inspected_files: spacewar_2b_25mar62.txt: comments and labels 1-1099; sections 85-135, 295-345, 572-782, 819-1060 at control-flow level
cut.note: a real-time simulation in a fixed instruction budget: every active object (two ships, torpedoes, explosions) is a row in parallel tables (x, y, dx, dy, angle, angular velocity, fuel, torpedoes, outline, and a POINTER TO ITS CALC ROUTINE); the main loop walks the tables, compares every pair for collision within an epsilon, then calls each object's calc routine to move and display it, and burns the remaining time budget so a frame takes constant time; an object changes behaviour by having its calc-routine pointer replaced (a ship that collides becomes an explosion with a duration count); the starfield is a background program; gravity toward the central star is a switch-selectable calc term

organs.human_name: main control routine 572-631 (the table set-up: mx1 x, my1 y, ma1 count, mb1 instruction count, mdx/mdy, mom angular velocity, mth angle, mal angular acceleration, mas, mfu fuel, mtr torpedoes, mot outline, mco control word, ml1 calc routine); 727-730 'yes, EXPLODE / replace calc routine with explosion / duration of explosion'; 993-998 'search for unused object'
organs.mechanism: nnn object slots hold one entry per table; a slot is active if its calc-routine word is non-zero; the ship, torpedo and explosion behaviours are separate routines and an object's identity IS which routine its slot points to; launching a torpedo finds an unused slot and fills it with the torpedo routine, a position and a life count; a collision overwrites the slot's routine with the explosion routine and sets a duration; when the duration or life count expires the slot is freed
assumptions: a small fixed number of objects; dispatch through a stored address is cheaper than a type field and a switch on a 1962 machine
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: new object kinds are new routines; the main loop never changes (the comment 'here put more bells and whistles, like hyperspace')
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: no free slot means a halt (998 'hlt / no space for new objects')
organs.human_prior: the earliest known instance of per-object behaviour dispatch in a game; the entity-table pattern
organs.source_boundary: the table definitions and the two pointer-replacement sites

organs.human_name: 683-782: the comparison loop (mx1/mx2 delta x, abs, epsilon me1/me2; 'yes, EXPLODE'), the calc-and-display loop (mq4 'routine for calculating spaceship or other object and displaying it'; mb1 'alter count of number of instructions'), 778-781 'display stars of the heavens / display massive star / use up rest of time of main loop / repeat whole works'
organs.mechanism: per frame: for every active object compare its x and y with every later active object; if both differences are under an epsilon (10000 octal, halved) both become explosions; then for every active object call its calc routine (which moves it, handles controls, draws its outline) and account the instructions it used; then draw the background starfield and the central star and spin in a counted loop until the frame's instruction budget is spent, so the simulation runs at a constant rate regardless of how many objects are active
assumptions: the machine is fast enough for the worst case within the budget; a constant frame time makes velocities meaningful
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: real-time interaction with deterministic physics on a 1962 machine
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: O(n^2) collision checks (fine for nnn objects); a frame that exceeds the budget slows the game rather than dropping objects
organs.human_prior: the fixed-timestep game loop; this is among its first instances
organs.source_boundary: the main loop ml0 to 'repeat whole works'

organs.human_name: spaceship calc 838-945 (ss1/ss2; angular velocity, thrust along the heading, 'switch 2 for heavy star' 907, fuel mfu); the sine-cosine subroutine 85-135 (Adams Associates, a polynomial with quadrant folding); torpedo calc 819-835 and 1002-1035 (velocity = ship velocity plus muzzle velocity along the heading; 'life of torpedo' 300 frames; 'permit torp tubes to cool'); star collision 1042-1060 ('spaceship in star'; switch 5 to escape)
organs.mechanism: each frame a ship integrates angular velocity into its heading, adds thrust (fuel permitting) along the heading via sine and cosine of the angle, adds an inverse-square pull toward the central star when the heavy-star switch is on, and integrates velocity into position with wrap-around; a torpedo is launched with the ship's velocity plus a fixed speed along the heading and lives for a fixed count; a ship entering the star is destroyed unless a console switch extracts it; the sine/cosine routine is a shared subroutine with a calling sequence documented in the comments
assumptions: first-order Euler integration at the frame rate is stable enough for play; gravity is optional because the 1961 version had none (Edwards added it)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: the orbital mechanics that made the game a game (the record: 'gravity by Dan Edwards')

pressures.source_evidence: the main control routine 572-782; the object tables
pressures.condition: an organism updates and displays n moving objects, some created and destroyed at run time, within a fixed instruction budget per frame; velocities must mean the same thing whatever n is; behaviour differs per object kind
pressures.resource_or_constraint: the frame's instruction count; nnn object slots
pressures.failure_condition: frame time that varies with n (velocities change), or a dispatch cost that grows with the number of kinds
pressures.world_punishes: a type switch per object; variable frame time
pressures.world_rewards: a stored routine pointer per object and a burned remainder
pressures.observable_consequence: frame time vs number of active objects, and per-object dispatch cost vs number of kinds, on a PDP-1 emulator
pressures.vacuity_condition: one object kind and a fixed n
pressures.trivial_shortcuts: a faster machine (which changes the game's speed unless the budget is enforced)
pressures.cheat_control: an organism with unlimited instructions must show constant frame time at any n; the loop without the burn must show frame time falling as objects explode; a switch-based dispatch must show cost growing with kinds: the world must show all three
pressures.purpose_separated_from_pressure: PURPOSE: real-time two-player simulation (Russell, Graetz, Wiitanen, Samson, Edwards 1961-62)
